source: Mehle (1980) Hypothesis generation in an automobile malfunction inference task (PhD dissertation, Univ. of Oklahoma)
finding: Experts and novices each listed only about 3.4 hypotheses per car-trouble problem. Experts did not list more than novices. Subjects seemed to stop when they had filled about a memory span of hypotheses.
numbers: N=12 (6 expert: 1 ex-mechanic student + 5 motor-pool staff; 6 novice undergraduates), 5 car-trouble problems each. Mean hypotheses per problem: novices 3.43, experts 3.36. Unacceptable hypotheses: 7 in total, about 0.1 per subject per problem.
quote: subjects appeared to adopt the strategy of generating enough hypotheses to fill a 'memory span'
limits: Tiny sample. Expert group is mostly motor-pool staff, not repair-shop diagnosticians. Subjects typed hypotheses on a keyboard, so effort cost may cap the count. Instruction was 'all plausible hypotheses you would entertain'.
agent_relevance: Humans stop at about 3 to 4 candidates whatever their skill. A scaffold that holds the candidate list in code removes this cap. Do not trust the model's own sense that its list is complete.

source: Mehle (1980) dissertation, pooled-set permutation analysis and simple sampling model
finding: Pooling all 12 subjects gave 17.8 distinct hypotheses per problem, but one subject produced only 19.2 percent of that pool. A sampling-without-replacement model (fixed N available hypotheses, each subject finds a fixed share S of the unfound ones) fit the pooling curve and put the true set near 21.5, so even 12 people missed about 3.7 per problem.
numbers: Pooled distinct hypotheses per problem: novices 12.6, experts 11.2, combined 17.8. Model fit: novice N=18.1, S=0.179 (predicted 3.24 vs observed 3.43); combined N=21.5. Slope of the pooling curve at 12 subjects was still about 1 new hypothesis per added person.
quote: the typical subject generated less than one-fifth of the possible hypotheses
limits: Reference set is the group pool, not an omniscient mechanic, so 19.2 percent is an upper bound on coverage. Model assumes equal chance per hypothesis, which ignores that strong hypotheses are found first. Hypotheses in the model are counted by their wording, not by cause.
agent_relevance: A direct way to measure our agent's coverage: pool many independent samples, fit the same capture curve, and read off how much one sample misses. Supports many independent short attempts with the union held in code (G4, G12).

source: Mehle (1980) dissertation, probability estimates and the 'they can't all be right' test
finding: Subjects judged their short lists to hold the true cause with high probability. Treating the estimates as probabilities of exclusive causes, the pooled estimates summed to far above 100 percent, so people were overconfident that the list was complete.
numbers: Mean stated probability that the true cause is in their list: novices 69.2 percent (range 17 to 98), experts 67.5 percent (range 27 to 100). Pooled adjusted estimate over the group's hypotheses: 504 percent (limit is 100).
quote: The typical subject generated quite impoverished sets of hypotheses, yet assessed their hypothesis sets as nearly exhaustive.
limits: The adjustment assumes missing hypotheses carry the mean probability of the included ones. Assumes hypotheses are mutually exclusive. The 504 percent figure is an upper estimate and is not a measure of per-person calibration.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-checkable test for our agent: if the model's stated probabilities over its candidates plus 'other' do not add to 100, or if it gives under 20 percent to 'not on my list', it is overconfident (G5 normalising in code).

source: Mehle (1980) dissertation, protocol analysis and expert versus novice content
finding: Think-aloud protocols were sparse, especially for experts. Subjects checked each hypothesis against the data as they generated it and threw out those that did not fit. They produced hypotheses in bursts, with data restatement between bursts. Experts named more specific parts; novices named causal chains that only link to the symptom indirectly.
numbers: Protocol units per problem: novices mean 33.4 (range 7 to 194), experts 15.6 (range 2 to 66). Medians over 5 problems: experts 54, novices 80.5. One expert subject produced 244 units, one novice 539 (outliers).
quote: The sparseness of experts' verbalizations, in comparison to novices, was unexpected.
limits: Only the two most verbal subjects were analysed in depth. Think-aloud may not capture fast memory retrieval. Expert/novice split rests on job, not tested skill.
agent_relevance: Generation is a quick memory pull plus a consistency filter. For our agent the filter is the place to put code: reject hypotheses that contradict stated facts, but keep a log of what was rejected and why (so a rejected one can return if the datum proves unreliable).

source: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein (1978) Fault trees: sensitivity of estimated failure probabilities to problem representation. J Exp Psychol: Human Perception and Performance 4(2), 330-344
finding: People shown a car-won't-start fault tree with major branches deleted gave far too little weight to 'all other problems'. Out of sight meant out of mind. They gave the branches they saw more of the blame instead.
numbers: Exp 1, N=148 paid student volunteers (unpruned tree n=93; pruned tree 1 n=29 lacking starting, ignition and mischief branches; pruned tree 2 n=26 lacking battery, fuel and engine). 'Other' should have risen from .078 to .468 in pruned tree 1; it rose only to .140. Pruned tree 2: should be .611, was .227. Only 1 of 55 pruned-tree subjects gave 'other' as much as it should be.
quote: Pruned tree subjects clearly did not appreciate how much had been left out
limits: Subjects had to give proportions on a pre-made tree, not generate causes. Self-rated expertise did not help. The failure-per-1000 measure was noisy, which the authors say themselves.
agent_relevance: Core result for 'availability' of omitted causes. If we show the model a candidate list, it will under-reserve for the unlisted. Our code should force a fixed reserve for 'none of these' and test it against sibling lists.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein (1978) fault trees, Experiment 2 (focus on 'all other') and Experiment 6 (garage mechanics)
finding: Telling subjects to think hard about what is missing helped only a little. Experienced mechanics were just as insensitive as students.
numbers: Exp 2, N=82: 'other' for pruned tree 1 rose from .140 to .217 (t(49)=1.88) and pruned tree 2 from .227 to .346 (t(58)=1.81), still far below .468 and .611. Exp 6: 29 of 60 mailed questionnaires returned (16 pruned, 13 unpruned), mechanics with 2 to 43 years of experience. Deleted branches plus 'other' should be .441; pruned-tree mechanics gave 'other' a mean of .215 (U z=2.87), median .16 vs .47. Experience and self-rated skill did not predict detection (tau=.058).
quote: neither self-rated degree of knowledge nor actual experience had any systematic relation to ability to detect what was missing
limits: Mail survey, 48 percent return, 29 mechanics in total. Mechanics had no incentive to be careful.
agent_relevance: Prompting 'consider what else could be there' gives a partial fix at best (about +50 percent of a too-small number). This supports G1: do not rely on self-reminders. Use external generators (other samples, a taxonomy of subsystems) to enumerate the unlisted.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein (1978) fault trees, Experiments 3 to 5 (detail level and splitting)
finding: More detail on the tree changed judgments only a little, and 'other' shrank slightly as detail grew. Splitting one branch into two parts made it look more important: a presentation effect, not new information.
numbers: Exp 3: 'other' fell monotonically with detail level, linear trend F(1,141)=7.40, p<.01; battery and fuel were judged more likely when given extra detail (t=2.95 for battery vs level 2). Splitting a branch raised its share by .066 in the cited comparison, about twice what more categories alone would give.
limits: Only one domain (car starting). Student samples. Exp 4 and 5 details were only skimmed in the opened text.
agent_relevance: How the candidate list is written (finer split of one subsystem) shifts the model's weights. Code should present candidates in a canonical, balanced granularity, or average across several partitions.

source: Elstein (2009) Thinking about diagnostic thinking: a 30-year perspective. Adv Health Sci Educ 14(Suppl 1), 7-18
finding: Retrospective by the lead author of the Elstein, Shulman and Sprafka (1978) studies. Physicians generated a small set of hypotheses from a few early findings and held three to five at once, though they could list more. Experts were not more accurate than non-experts in that sample. Rapid pattern recognition that is wrong is a special case of premature closure.
numbers: 'between three and five diagnostic hypotheses were considered simultaneously' (the 'magic number 4 +/- 1'). General internists and family physicians; experts picked by peer ratings.
quote: between three and five diagnostic hypotheses were considered simultaneously, although any physician in our sample could easily enumerate more possibilities
limits: This is the author's summary, not the 1978 book. The small case sample could not separate experts from others. Counts were from think-aloud and simulated cases. The summary does not report the per-physician means.
agent_relevance: The count limit is a working-memory limit, not a knowledge limit (they could list more). A language model has no such limit on listing, so the structural cap is a design choice we can lift in code, with the model only asked to propose, not to hold.

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature. BMJ 324, 729-732
finding: Review of 30 years of diagnosis research. Good diagnosticians generate a limited number of hypotheses early. Failure to generate the right hypothesis is a leading error type in hard cases. Commitment to a hypothesis makes restructuring harder. Other documented errors: reading findings as consistent with one hypothesis, forgetting facts that contradict the favoured one, over-weighting positive findings, anchoring with insufficient adjustment.
numbers: No new counts. States later-presented information gets more weight than earlier (order effect, ref 25).
quote: Many diagnostic problems are so complex that the correct solution is not contained in the initial set of hypotheses.
limits: Narrative review. Strategy mattered less than content knowledge: both right and wrong diagnosticians used hypothesis testing.
agent_relevance: Gives the list of failure types to build checks for: missing-hypothesis, confirmation, ignoring contradicting facts. Also warns that the same strategy is used by good and poor solvers, so knowing the schema is not enough; coverage and checks have to be enforced.

source: Kourtidis, Nurek, Delaney & Kostopoulou (2022) Influences of early diagnostic suggestions on clinical reasoning. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 7:103
finding: Giving family physicians a list of diagnostic suggestions at the start did not clearly change certainty, information search or diagnosis changes in three online experiments. When the suggested list contained the physician's own first diagnosis, they tended to be more certain and to request less information, as if the list was a stamp of approval.
numbers: Exp 2: 194 analysed of 217 family physicians; diagnosis changed 50.0 percent with suggestions vs 46.9 percent without (OR=1.196, p=.389); certainty fell 0.85 on a 0-10 scale overall. Exp 3 (273 recruited, 248 analysed; changes 15.5 percent overall): diagnosis changed more when the likely diagnosis was left out of the list than when it was in (OR=2.143, p=.018) but not vs control (OR=0.960, p=.769). Initial certainty predicted fewer changes (OR=0.623 to 0.799) and fewer cues requested.
quote: when physicians see their focal diagnosis in the list of suggestions, they may become closed- rather than open-minded
limits: Mostly non-significant trends. Online vignettes with hypothetical aid. Earlier studies by the same group (Kostopoulou 2015a,b, 2017) did find accuracy gains from early suggestions. Mechanism is unproven.
agent_relevance: Supplying a hypothesis list is not a clean fix. A list that confirms the model's first guess may harden it. Safer: generate the list before the model commits, hide the model's own first guess from the check step, and use the list only for the test plan.

source: Sprenger, Dougherty, Atkins, Franco-Watkins, Thomas, Lange & Abbs (2011) Implications of cognitive load for hypothesis generation and probability judgment. Frontiers in Psychology 2:129
finding: Dividing attention while judging raised subadditivity. Dividing attention while learning the material lowered the number of hypotheses later generated, and that lowered number fully explained the later bias in probability judgments. Fewer hypotheses in the set means the target hypothesis gets more probability.
numbers: Three experiments. HyGene simulation: working-memory capacity set to 2 vs 4 hypotheses; encoding L=0.5 to 0.9; 1,000 trials per cell. Result: the effect of encoding load on judgment was completely mediated by the number of hypotheses generated.
quote: limitations in both encoding and recall can cascade into biases in judgments
limits: Student participants, learned stimuli (not real expertise). One prediction of HyGene (that load at encoding would not matter) was wrong.
agent_relevance: The mechanism chain matters for our design: set size feeds judgment. If the candidate set is small, probabilities on each member are inflated. Judge candidates only after the code has widened the set.

source: Lange, Thomas & Davelaar (2012) Temporal dynamics of hypothesis generation: the influences of data serial order, data consistency, and elicitation timing. Frontiers in Psychology 3:215
finding: In a simulated medical diagnosis, which hypothesis comes to mind depends on the order in which the symptoms arrive. Later data weighed more. People generated fewer than two hypotheses on average. A HyGene extension with a working-memory buffer of data explained the order effect.
numbers: Exp 1: N=72 University of Oklahoma students, within-subject symptom order, 4 cues. Mean hypotheses generated per order condition ranged 1.67 to 1.89, with no difference between orders (F(3,68)=0.567, p=.64).
limits: Students and an invented disease ecology. Recency in generation can flip to primacy under fast presentation, per the model.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence in the prompt changes what the model proposes. Code should shuffle or repeat fact order across independent attempts, then union the hypotheses.

source: Mehle (1980) dissertation, introduction: the Oklahoma hypothesis-generation programme it builds on
finding: The dissertation places itself in an ONR-funded line of work by Gettys, Fisher, Manning, Baca and Mehle. Earlier tasks (guess an unseen student's major from classes taken) also gave very small hypothesis sets. Gettys and Fisher (1979) proposed an executive process that starts, steers and stops recursive memory searches, and restarts retrieval when the plausibility of the current set is low. Mehle et al. (1979) pinned the overconfidence on an availability heuristic.
numbers: No new counts in this passage. Cites Gettys, Mehle, Baca, Fisher & Manning (1979) 'impoverished sets'; Fisher et al. (1979) consistency checking; Gettys et al. (1979) memory retrieval aid.
quote: the stimulus for initiation of hypothesis generation would be low plausibility of the current hypothesis set
limits: Second-hand description of technical reports that I could not open (DTIC copy returned 403). Technical reports, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: The Gettys-Fisher rule is a stop/restart rule: search again only when plausibility of the current set is low. Same shape as G1 (doubt on a signal). The weakness is that the plausibility judgment itself is biased upward (a03), so the trigger must be a code check, not the model's feeling.

source: Mehle (1980) dissertation, expert versus novice hypothesis content and the counting heuristic
finding: Experts named specific faulty parts (for example a neutral safety switch) tied directly to the complaint. Novices named parts that only affect the symptom indirectly (alternator, voltage regulator). The author reads this as experts retrieving more and keeping a few specific ones, versus novices reaching for causal chains to fill a quota. One expert's protocol suggests the probability estimate came from how long the list looked, not what was on it.
numbers: Protocol lines: expert F100-F103 'at least fifty percent ... that's a lot of stuff'; F242-F244 'at least seventy-five percent with all that stuff there'. Based on the two most verbal subjects only.
quote: 'a lot' appeared to be functionally related to 'very probable'
limits: Two subjects' protocols, single coder. The counting-heuristic reading is the author's guess from a few lines.
agent_relevance: List length can stand in for coverage in the generator's mind. A model that writes a long, fluent list may feel complete. Code should measure coverage by the union across independent attempts, not by the length of one list.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein (1978) fault trees, theory section and rule of thumb
finding: The authors set three explanations against each other for pruned-tree behaviour: credibility (spotting an omission discredits the whole tree and inflates the missing share), availability (what is not mentioned is not thought of), and accurate internal frequency knowledge. The data fit availability best. They give a rule of thumb: the missing share grows with how many missing things you can think of and with your unfamiliarity with the system.
numbers: See a05. Unpruned subjects gave 'other' .078 (Exp 1) and .067 (Exp 2).
quote: The proportion of missing sources of trouble is proportional to the number of things I can think of that are missing multiplied by a measure of my general familiarity with the system.
limits: The rule of thumb is a suggestion, not tested. True 'other' shares are unknown, since the tree was built from manuals and mechanics.
agent_relevance: The 'other' bucket is systematically underweighted. Code can enforce a minimum reserve for unlisted causes and raise it when the problem is unfamiliar (low prior success, G12).

source: Elstein (2009) 30-year perspective, errors and premature closure
finding: Early hypotheses are needed to limit the problem space, but they bring the risk of premature closure. The solver may read neutral cues as support for the favoured hypothesis, or fail to use data to test competing hypotheses. Wrong pattern recognition is called a special case of premature closure.
numbers: No counts. Cites Klayman (1995) and Wolf, Gruppen & Billi (1985) for neutral-cue reading and for not testing competing hypotheses.
quote: The formation of early hypotheses is essential to limit the problem space, but there is always the hazard of premature closure.
limits: Narrative review. Gives no rates of premature closure.
agent_relevance: Two checks to code: (1) rate each datum against every live candidate, not only the favoured one (G3); (2) log neutral cues as neutral and count them separately.

source: Thomas, Dougherty & Buttaccio (2014) Memory constraints on hypothesis generation and decision making. Current Directions in Psychological Science 23(4), 264-270
finding: Review of the HyGene programme. Three principles: data cue hypotheses from long-term memory; the number held in working memory is limited by capacity and task load; held hypotheses drive probability judgment and information search. If only one hypothesis is held, search must be confirmatory. If two or more are held, search can be diagnostic.
numbers: HyGene simulations (their figures 2 and 3): time pressure or lower working-memory capacity gives fewer hypotheses and a higher sum of probability judgments over exclusive hypotheses (subadditivity). Dougherty & Hunter (2003a,b): subadditivity correlated with working-memory capacity; low-capacity people behaved as though they held fewer hypotheses.
quote: If only one hypothesis is maintained in working memory, then hypothesis-guided search necessarily follows a confirmation-search strategy
limits: Review by the model's authors. Many results are simulation or student lab tasks with learned stimuli. The claim that held-hypothesis count sets the search type rests on one study cited as in-press work (Thomas, Lange & Dougherty).
agent_relevance: Strongest theory link to our schema: breadth of the held set decides whether tests are diagnostic. Keep at least two live candidates in every test-selection step, with code choosing the test that splits them (links to the Probing and measurement selection subfield).

source: Thomas, Dougherty & Buttaccio (2014), order effects and speed of data
finding: The same datum changes which hypothesis is generated depending on where it sits in the sequence. Late data counted more (recency) in a one-informative-cue design. Fast presentation, harder tasks and higher capacity pushed toward primacy (first data counted more).
numbers: Lange, Thomas & Davelaar (2012b): one informative cue among three uninformative ones, placed in each of 4 serial positions; later positions contributed more. Lange et al. (2013): 5 symptoms, first two favour disease A, last two disease B; slow presentation gave recency, fast gave primacy.
quote: the same datum can have different impacts on which hypotheses are generated depending on where it is presented in the sequence
limits: Student participants, artificial disease sets. Direction (recency or primacy) depends on pace and load, so there is no single rule.
agent_relevance: The order of facts in the prompt is a hidden variable. Run independent attempts with facts shuffled, then merge candidates in code (G4: samples from one model are not independent, so vary the input, not just the seed).

source: Lange (2011) Hypothesis Generation: Temporal Dynamics (PhD dissertation, Univ. of Oklahoma)
finding: When new data contradicted the hypotheses held, people dropped those hypotheses from working memory. They did not go back to long-term memory for new ones. Elicitation only at the end showed primacy, while step-by-step elicitation in Experiment 1 showed recency. Cited prior work says people use only a subset of available cues.
numbers: Experiment 2 conclusion: clear evidence for purging inconsistent hypotheses, no evidence of re-cueing long-term memory. Fisher & Gettys (1987) estimate quoted there: about 2 cues used when 3 are available, 3 when 4 are available.
quote: Clear evidence was found for the purging of inconsistent hypotheses from working memory
limits: Student samples; invented medical ecology. The Fisher & Gettys figure is cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: After a failed test the human drops candidates but does not search for new ones. In our loop a failed check (S4 to S5) must trigger fresh candidate generation in code, since the model's tendency, like the human one, is to prune and stop.

source: Mehlhorn, Taatgen, Lebiere & Krems (2011) Memory activation and the availability of explanations in sequential diagnostic reasoning. J Exp Psychol: LMC
finding: Two experiments measured how available each explanation was while symptoms arrived one at a time, using a reaction-time probe. Four ACT-R models were compared. The best model treated all observed symptoms as equal activators of explanations, with no decay. Memory activation alone gave about the right diagnosis when symptoms agreed, and people needed extra deliberate reasoning when symptoms did not pick one explanation.
numbers: Exp 1: 23 undergraduates (22 analysed), human diagnostic accuracy 95.5 percent (SD 3.7), diagnosis time 705 ms. Exp 2: 29 recruited (26 analysed), accuracy 95.9 percent (SD 3.9). Probe-RT fit R2: Exp 1 model-number .85, model-current .79, model-time .79, model-constant .70; Exp 2 model-number .71, model-constant .45, model-time .37, model-current .24.
quote: reasoners generate only a subset of up to four possible hypotheses from memory
limits: Artificial chemicals-and-symptoms learned for the study. Accuracy was high, so errors were rare. The 'up to four' line is the authors' summary of earlier work (Barrows 1982, Elstein 1978, Joseph & Patel 1990, Mehle 1982, Weber 1993).
agent_relevance: Independent restatement of the four-hypothesis cap and a rule for what is dropped: low-activation hypotheses. Suggests the model's candidates, like human ones, follow association strength, so rare but true causes are the ones lost.

source: Sprenger et al. (2011) Frontiers in Psychology 2:129, theory and Experiment 1 design
finding: The probability of a target hypothesis is judged by comparing its strength to the strength of alternatives retrieved at that moment (Tversky & Koehler support theory). Fewer retrieved alternatives gives a higher judgment, and judgments over exclusive options then sum to more than 100 percent. Earlier work found people retrieve strong, high-probability alternatives and that the count tracks working-memory span and generation time.
numbers: Exp 1: 167 participants; load task keeps 1, 4, 6 or 8 letters in mind; restaurant-menu learning task, menu frequencies 10-10-8-8-4-4-3-3 over 50 days; probability judgments in 10 percent steps. HyGene demo: working memory 2 vs 4 hypotheses; balanced vs unbalanced trace frequencies (10,5,5,4,4,4,4,1 vs 15,10,7,1,1,1,1,1).
limits: Lab learning of artificial menus, not expertise. Load at judgment had a clear effect, but the encoding-load prediction of HyGene failed.
agent_relevance: The subadditivity test (probabilities over exclusive options sum above 100) is a cheap, automatic way to detect an under-generated set. Add it as a code check on any model-stated probability table.

source: Kourtidis, Nurek, Delaney & Kostopoulou (2022), background on supplying early suggestions
finding: Earlier work by the same group found that early diagnostic suggestions raised accuracy in three studies (two online case studies in the UK and Greece, one high-fidelity simulation with actor-patients) without more consultation time or more investigations. The authors say the mechanism was untested, which is why they ran the three experiments in a10. They also describe consider-the-opposite as an effective debiasing strategy that decision aids can implement.
numbers: Prior studies: Kostopoulou et al. 2015a, 2015b, 2017a,b. Family physicians. No accuracy figures in this paper's introduction.
limits: Figures for those earlier studies were not in the opened text. The 2022 follow-up did not reproduce clear process effects.
agent_relevance: Supplying a list early helped accuracy in the field, but the reason is unknown and the 2022 follow-up warns of confirmation when the list echoes the first guess. Test in our harness: list supplied before vs after the model's first answer.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning (arXiv 2607.10275)
finding: In a staged haematology-oncology task where models request data across three rounds, 32 frontier models showed search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure, the same failure types seen in novice clinicians. Differential reasoning was the weakest component for every model. Fluent reasoning traces did not track accuracy.
numbers: 32 models, 20 cases, 3 rounds. Best model 68.1 percent overall. Gap between diagnostic accuracy and differential reasoning averaged 23.0 percentage points. Requests per round fell from 7.5 (SD 3.9) to 4.2 (SD 2.2) to 1.8 (SD 1.0). Utilisation (share of available data requested) correlated with accuracy R=0.69 and fell from 57 percent to 26 percent in the last round. 91 percent of reasoning traces scored above threshold on a rubric but decorrelated from accuracy.
quote: search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure as the dominant failure modes
limits: Preprint, July 2026, not peer reviewed. Scoring by an LLM judge, checked against one haematologist. Narrow domain. Results could shift with newer models.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence for narrowing: models ask for less data as they go and keep the first level of diagnosis. Supports forcing a minimum number of live candidates and a fixed information-request budget per round in code (G12).

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing diagnostic accuracy through multi-agent conversations: using LLMs to mitigate cognitive bias (arXiv 2401.14589, JMIR)
finding: GPT-4 agents given roles (decider, devil's advocate for anchoring and confirmation, facilitator for premature closure, summariser) were run on 16 case reports in which bias had caused a real misdiagnosis. The first answer was always wrong (selected that way). After discussion the top differential was right in most runs.
numbers: 80 simulations (16 cases). Initial diagnosis accuracy 0 percent (0/80). Top differential after discussion 71.3 percent (57/80). Two final differentials 80.0 percent (64/80).
limits: Abstract-level read through a summariser. Cases were picked because a human was misled, so 0 percent at baseline is by design. No per-bias breakdown and no plain-model resampling control at equal cost. Our G9 says debate gains are mostly extra sampling.
agent_relevance: Suggests the first LLM answer on bias-prone cases is wrong and that more candidates help. The design lacks a matched-sample control, so treat it as weak support for breadth, not for debate roles.

source: Weber, Boeckenholt, Hilton & Wallace (1993) Determinants of diagnostic hypothesis generation: effects of information, base rates, and experience. J Exp Psychol: LMC 19(5), 1151-1164
finding: Physicians generated diagnoses for case histories with two plausible diagnoses that differed in base rate and severity. Order and frequency of generation followed the amount of information and the base rate, with little base-rate neglect. A diagnosis recently seen in a similar case came earlier and more often. Experience acted only by raising the availability of similar cases.
numbers: Abstract only (via Europe PMC summary); sample size and counts not read.
quote: Physicians' experience affected hypothesis generation solely by increasing the availability of similar cases
limits: Abstract-level read through a summariser. Full text not opened. Task had two target diagnoses.
agent_relevance: Generation is driven by recent and frequent cases. For a language model the analogue is prompt-recent examples and training frequency. Rare-but-severe causes need an explicit generator (taxonomy sweep) rather than waiting for them to appear.

source: Graber, Franklin & Gordon (2005) Diagnostic error in internal medicine. Arch Intern Med 165(13), 1493-1499
finding: Review of 100 diagnostic error cases in internal medicine. Cognitive causes appeared in most cases, and premature closure was the single most common one. Faulty knowledge was uncommon.
numbers: 100 cases (33 deaths). Cognitive factors in 74 percent and system factors in 65 percent (from a secondary summary of the abstract).
quote: Premature closure, ie, the failure to continue considering reasonable alternatives after an initial diagnosis was reached
limits: Abstract-level read through search and summariser. Cases came from autopsy discrepancies, quality assurance and voluntary reports, so selection and hindsight bias apply. Not a rate of error in practice.
agent_relevance: Gives a base rate for failure type: not missing knowledge but not continuing. Code can enforce a rule that no answer is accepted while only one live candidate has been tested.

source: Rouse (1978) Human problem solving performance in a fault diagnosis task. IEEE Trans SMC 8, 258-270
finding: Two experiments on diagnosing faults in graphically displayed networks. Human performance fell short of optimal as problems grew. Forced pacing pushed people toward brute-force strategies. A computer aid that did the bookkeeping cut incorrect diagnoses substantially.
numbers: Abstract only (NASA NTRS record): factors varied were problem size, forced pacing, computer aiding, training. No numbers read.
limits: Abstract-level read through a summariser; no full text at the NASA record. Mehle (1980) cites Rouse 1978a,b and a fuzzy-set model of the same task. Network tasks are abstract, not real equipment.
agent_relevance: Bookkeeping is what humans do worst and code does best: tracking which candidates are alive. Early evidence for the schema rule that code, not the model, holds the candidate list.

source: Barrows, Norman, Neufeld & Feightner (1982) The clinical reasoning of randomly selected physicians in general medical practice. Clin Invest Med 5(1), 49-55
finding: Observed simulated patient encounters of randomly chosen family physicians and internists. Physicians formed several diagnostic hypotheses early in the encounter and used them to direct questions. Accuracy and promptness of hypothesis generation were linked to diagnostic accuracy.
numbers: 18 family physicians and 19 general internists, 62 encounters across 4 standardised simulated patient problems (from a search-result abstract).
limits: Read from a search snippet only. No hypothesis counts found. Page not opened.
agent_relevance: Early generation quality predicts accuracy, so the first candidate set is the bottleneck; spend budget on generating it widely, not on polishing the first guess.

source: Sprafka (1973) dissertation on hypothesis-generation instructions (Michigan State), as described in a library record
finding: A thesis that varied instructions to physicians: generate diagnostic hypotheses early, withhold judgment until the end, or no instruction. It measured number of hypotheses, thoroughness and efficiency of cue acquisition, and accuracy.
numbers: No results seen. Only the design was described in search output.
limits: Download failed (returned an HTML page, not the thesis). Results unknown.
agent_relevance: The early-versus-withhold-judgment contrast is an experiment worth repeating with a language model: force listing before testing, versus allow the first guess to start the test.
